questions.problem:
$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-1, & x\in [-\pi ,0] \\ 3, & x\in (0,\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=\pi .$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=\pi .$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}f(x)=3 \\ {f}^{+}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}f(x)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(\pi )+{f}^{+}(\pi )}{2}=\frac{3+(-1)}{2}=1.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}, & x\in [-\pi ,0] \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x+1, & x\in (0,\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
f\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2})+1=2.
$$

Consider the function $F(x)=|x|$ defined on $x\in [-2,2).$ The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼1-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}(2n-1)^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{2}x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

At $x=0,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{2}\cdot 0)={{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is 
{{field-2}}
at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(0)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}={{field-4}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our Fourier series as

$$
f(x)∼1-\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{2}x).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{2}\cdot 0)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(0)=0.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =1-\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{2}\cdot 0) \\ 0 & =1-\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}\cdot 1 \\ -1 & =-\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}} & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $F(x)=x$ defined on $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ).$ The Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

At $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})={{field-1}}.
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})={{field-2}}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is 
{{field-3}}
at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2})={{field-4}}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}={{field-5}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we separate the Fourier series into its odd and even terms as follows:

$$
f(x)∼2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((2n-1)x)-2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2nx).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=(-1)^{n+1}.
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=0.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot (-1)^{n+1}-2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n}\cdot 0 \\ \frac{\pi }{4} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
